paragraphs.text: Goldfarb et al. (1998) described desmin-related myopathy as a familial disorder in which skeletal muscle weakness occurs with cardiac conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and restrictive heart failure, and with intracytoplasmic accumulation of desmin-reactive deposits in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. Vajsar et al. (1993) associated this rare familial myopathy with an unusual distribution of desmin intermediate filament proteins in skeletal muscle and probably also in cardiac muscle. van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) described desmin-related myopathy as an autosomally inherited skeletal and cardiac myopathy, caused mainly by dominant mutations in the DES gene.

paragraphs.text: Porte et al. (1980) reported 3 brothers with progressive myocardial deficiency. Cardiac muscle cells stored PAS-negative proteinaceous material. On electron microscopy this material consisted of sinuous filaments, 7 to 10 nm in diameter, similar to the intermediate filaments normally present in cardiac muscle cells. Cardiac muscle cells also showed myofibrillar disintegration with Z-band changes and rod-like bodies, sarcoplasmic reticulum proliferation, and glycogen accumulation. Discrete sarcoplasmic reticulum proliferation, glycogen overload, and filament deposits were seen in a few skeletal muscle fibers.

paragraphs.text: Wolburg et al. (1982) reported 2 patients, both 32 years old, with a congenital disorder of the skeletal muscles. One patient (case 2) also had congenital paresis of the dilator muscle of the pupil and cardiomyopathy. Muscle biopsies showed variation in fiber caliber, with grouped atrophic fibers in case 1. Cytoplasmic bodies were present in about a third of fibers in case 1 and about a tenth of fibers in case 2, together with Z-disk streaming and subsarcolemmal filamentous bodies. The inclusions consisted of dense granular and fine filamentous components consistent with cytoplasmic bodies. The authors noted that cytoplasmic bodies are a nonspecific type of inclusion but were the outstanding structural anomaly in both patients. The course ended in severe impairment of skeletal muscle function in case 1 but not in case 2.

paragraphs.text: Abe et al. (1993) described a Japanese kindred with an autosomal dominant progressive myopathy with diffuse cytoplasmic bodies. Across 4 successive generations, 12 patients had weakness and atrophy of the muscles of the distal extremities, neck, thorax, and shoulder girdles. Mean age at onset was 42 years, and patients became disabled 5 to 10 years after onset because of chronic respiratory failure. Males were affected about twice as often as females. Serum creatine kinase was normal or slightly elevated, and electromyography was myopathic with slight neurogenic change. Autopsy of 2 patients showed numerous cytoplasmic bodies in skeletal muscle, predominantly in type I fibers, and smooth and cardiac muscle were also affected. Electron microscopy showed dense central cores of myofilaments with radiating filaments.

paragraphs.text: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994) described a large family with autosomal dominant distal myopathy with desmin storage. The disease began in early to middle adulthood with gait disturbance due to distal leg weakness. Over 5 to 10 years it progressed to involve all extremities and the bulbar, respiratory, and facial muscles. Cardiac involvement was frequent, with arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and congestive heart failure, and led to premature death. Muscle biopsies from multiple family members at different stages of disease showed desmin storage and autophagocytosis. Electromyography showed prominent spontaneous activity, short-duration motor unit potentials, and polyphasia.

paragraphs.text: Ariza et al. (1995) reported a 28-year-old man with generalized muscular atrophy, cardiomyopathy, intestinal malabsorption, and intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Abundant sarcoplasmic granular and filamentous aggregates that were continuous with Z lines or dense bodies and stained intensely for desmin were present throughout the skeletal musculature, the myocardium, and the smooth muscle of the intestine. Neurofilament-immunoreactive axonal spheroids were also found in the spinal cord and roots. The authors concluded that desmin myopathy is a multisystem disorder. They described intestinal smooth muscle involvement for the first time and considered the coexisting neurofilament aggregates an extremely rare combination of intermediate filament pathology in the neuromuscular system.

paragraphs.text: Melberg et al. (1999) investigated 21 members of a Swedish family with myopathy and cardiomyopathy. Twelve patients had myopathy, and electromyography was myopathic in 10. Weakness was axial in mildly affected patients, axial and mainly distal in moderately affected patients, and generalized in severely affected patients. Muscle biopsies showed rimmed vacuoles and accumulation of desmin, dystrophin, and other proteins, and electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous changes and myofibrillar disorganization. Some patients had episodes of chest pain and palpitations. paragraphs.text: Pinol-Ripoll et al. (2009) reported a girl, the only child of consanguineous parents (uncle and niece), who had recurrent syncope from the age of 6 months. The episodes were first attributed to a right posteroseptal accessory conduction pathway and later diagnosed as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. She also had cyanotic attacks. On examination she had a long narrow face, bilateral facial weakness, ptosis, scapular winging, and atrophy of the masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid, and trunk muscles. She also had pes cavus, shoulder girdle weakness, distal weakness of the upper and lower extremities, and hypoactive deep tendon reflexes. Sensation was normal and there was no clinical myotonia. Creatine kinase was twice normal. Electromyography showed low-amplitude motor potentials, complex repetitive and myotonic discharges, and a myopathic pattern. Cardiac findings included monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, QT prolongation, second-degree AV block, ventricular fibrillation, mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 45%), right ventricular dilatation, marked atrial enlargement, and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss suggested involvement of intestinal smooth muscle. Brain MRI was normal. Muscle biopsy showed variation in fiber size, subsarcolemmal desmin-reactive aggregates, and rimmed vacuoles, with granulofilamentous material on electron microscopy. She died of cardiac failure. The authors considered this the first reported case of infantile-onset desmin-associated cardiomyopathy.
